steps.body: The theorem's real power is selective. If you want only the b³ term of (a + b)⁷, you need not expand the other seven — set k = 3 and write C(7,3)·a⁴·b³. The whole skill is deciding what k is, and reading it off the power of b every time.
Which region is which, when the constants differ.

widget.prompt: Build (x + 4)(x + 2) and read the CONSTANT term — the corner alone.
widget.successFeedback: x² + 6x + 8. The corner is 4×2 = 8 and the strips add to 6x — selecting one region is exactly what ‘find a single term’ asks you to do.
widget.productMiddleFeedback: That reads the strips instead of the corner. The corner multiplies the two partitions: 4×2 = 8.
widget.partialFeedback: One partition has not arrived — this rectangle is 4 down and 2 across.
widget.signFeedback: Both partitions are added here, so both stay positive.

predict.prompt: In (a + b)⁷, which k gives the term containing b³?
predict.reveal: k IS the exponent on b, always — so b³ means k = 3 and the coefficient is C(7,3) = 35. Reading k off the power of a instead is harmless: C(7,4) = C(7,3) by symmetry, for every n. The slip that bites is POSITION — b³ sits in the fourth term, and using 4 as k happens to give 35 here only because 4 = 7 − 3. In (a + b)⁸ the same position slip gives C(8,4) = 70 instead of 56.

explanationVariants: b³ in (a + b)⁷ means k = 3, so the coefficient is C(7,3) = 35.
The a-power is then 7 − 3 = 4, and 4 + 3 = 7 checks out.

widget.prompt: In (a + b)⁷, what is the coefficient of a⁴b³?

commonErrors.feedback: 21 is C(7,2). The b-power here is 3, so k = 3, not 2.
7 is C(7,1), the coefficient of a⁶b. Match k to the exponent on b.

widget.successFeedback: 35 — and C(7,4) is also 35, which is why this particular case forgives the wrong reasoning. The next one will not.

steps.body: Because rows are symmetric, C(n,k) and C(n,n−k) agree — so reading k off the power of a instead of b always returns the very same coefficient. The slip that DOES cost you is position: the b³ term sits FOURTH in the expansion, but its k is 3. Using the position as k only matches by luck, when the position happens to equal n − k. Anchor k to the power of b and luck never enters.

explanationVariants: b³ in (a + b)⁸ means k = 3, so the coefficient is C(8,3) = 56.
C(8,3) = 56, while C(8,4) = 70 — here the two disagree.

widget.prompt: In (a + b)⁸, what is the coefficient of a⁵b³?

commonErrors.feedback: 70 is C(8,4) — the POSITION of the b³ term (fourth) was used as k. The exponent on b is the k: k = 3, and C(8,3) = 56.

widget.fallbackFeedback: k = 3, so the coefficient is C(8,3) = 56.
widget.successFeedback: 56 — and note that C(8,4) = 70 is a different number entirely. Anchoring k to b is what protects you.

explanationVariants: Terms are numbered from k = 0, so the term with k = 3 is the fourth one.
k = 0 is the first term, so k = 3 is the fourth.

widget.prompt: Counting from the start, which term of (a + b)⁷ contains b³?

options.label: The 4th
options.feedback: Yes — k runs 0, 1, 2, 3, so k = 3 sits in fourth place.

options.label: The 3rd
options.feedback: That reads k as the position. Position is k + 1, because k starts at 0.

options.label: The 7th
options.feedback: The 7th term would be k = 6, giving b⁶.

explanationVariants: The x² term of (x + 3)⁵ is C(5,3)·x²·3³ = 10×27 = 270.
hints: Decide k first: which power of the constant 3 pairs with x² in (x + 3)⁵?
x² leaves three factors of 3, so k = 3 and the combination is C(5,3) = 10.

widget.prompt: In (x + 3)⁵, what is the coefficient of x²?

commonErrors.feedback: That is C(5,3) alone — the 3³ = 27 still has to multiply it.
That uses 3¹ instead of 3³. Three factors of the constant accompany x².

widget.successFeedback: 270 — one term extracted, four never computed.

steps.body: Pick the term, skip the rest.
takeaways: The general term is C(n,k)·aⁿ⁻ᵏ·bᵏ, with k read off the power of b.
Row symmetry can hide a wrong k — anchor it to b every time.
The term with exponent k sits in position k + 1.
steps.teaser: Next: let a and b be probabilities, and the expansion becomes a distribution.
